title: How the new harness joins each part that keeps its factory plug
ask: Where a part keeps its factory plug (the stalks, the light switch, the lamps, the wiper and pop-up motors), should that plug be cut off the old harness and spliced onto the new one - and if so, in the car as each circuit moves, or at the bench beforehand?
why:
Two standing things disagree. The device-end rule (carried from the old install plan) says: where a part keeps its factory plug - the stalks, the light switch, the lamps, the wiper and pop-up motors, the senders - cut that plug off the old harness with 150 mm of its wire and splice it onto the new leg. Your ruling D-411 says the old harness comes out uncut, is boxed, and is the fallback until after shakedown. Both cannot hold: a harness with its plugs cut off cannot simply be plugged back in.

The answer also fixes something no row says today: when the splicing happens - at the bench while each leg is built (E20-E23), or in the car as each circuit moves over (E28). The new legs are the same either way; what changes is where each last 150 mm comes from, where the splices are made, and when the old harness stops being whole.
options:
(a) Cut each plug off the old harness in the car, one circuit at a time, as that circuit moves over (E28), and splice it onto the new leg there. Costs nothing. The old harness stays whole and working until each circuit has been proven on the new one; after that it is a boxed harness without its plugs, and putting it back would mean splicing every plug on again. The splices are made in the car, some under the dash and at the nose.
(b) Cut every plug off before the legs are tested at the bench (E20-E23), so each leg is finished with its factory plugs on and tested whole in comfort. Costs nothing. The car stops running on the old harness weeks earlier, before the new one is proven, and there is no fallback from that day.
(c) Leave the old harness completely uncut and get a second set of mating plugs for the new legs - from a breaker's harness, since most are no longer sold new - or change a part's own lead to a new connector pair where it has a lead. The boxed harness stays plug-in ready, as D-411 pictured it. Costs money and a hunt nobody has priced, and a part whose plug is moulded into its body can only take the breaker's plug.
recommend: (a), unless a boxed harness that plugs straight back in matters more to you than the cost and the hunt for a second set of plugs - then (c)
stops: How each load is joined in the migration (E28, every circuit), the lead left at each leg end when the legs are built (E20 to E23), and whether E30 pulls the old harness intact or without its plugs. Nothing before the freeze waits on it.

title: Wipers and turn signals with the key out
ask: Should the wipers, washer and turn signals work only with the key on, as the factory car did, or whenever the car's electronics are awake?
why:
As the design stands, the wiper and turn-signal outputs have no key condition at all. With the key out, a stalk left on runs the wipers or flashes one side whenever the car's electronics are awake (opening a door wakes them), and the wipers stop wherever they are when the car goes back to sleep about 30 seconds later. Nobody ruled this; the key was simply left out of those rows.

The factory car fed the turn signals from the ignition position. Its wipers were key-fed too, but the car's own record reads their fuse as an accessory (ACC) feed in three places and as an ignition feed in one, so ACC or RUN for the wipers is part of the choice.

Hazards, horn, headlamps, parking lamps and brake lamps work with the key out today and are not part of this question. It is a setting in the power module: no wire and no part changes whichever you choose.
options:
(a) As the factory car, by its record: turn signals need the key in RUN; wipers and washer work from ACC upward. Nothing runs with the key out. Costs nothing.
(b) Everything needs RUN: wipers, washer and turn signals. The simplest rule; you cannot clear the screen while sitting with the key at ACC.
(c) Leave it as it is: wipers and turn signals work whenever the car is awake, key in or out. A wiper stalk left on sweeps a dry screen each time a door is opened and parks nowhere when the car sleeps; costs nothing, drains the battery a little faster while it runs.
recommend: (a), unless you want to be able to wipe the screen with the key out - then say (a) for the turn signals and (c) for the wipers
stops: The wiper and turn-signal rows of the logic table and the configuration entered into the power module at E25; E29's function check tests whichever is ruled. No wire, part or earlier row waits on it.

title: The pass figure for the cranking voltage-drop test
ask: What should count as a pass when the voltage drop on the new battery cables is measured while cranking?
why:
Today both readings must be under 0.5 V to pass: battery + to the starter stud (E43) and battery - to the engine block (E44), each taken while a helper cranks the engine. But the battery is in the back now, and 18 ft of the 1/0 cable chosen for each run drops 0.5 V by itself at about 280 A (the wire table gives 0.0983 ohm per 1000 ft). The starter is expected to pull 300 to 500 A, so a perfect cable with perfect crimps would read roughly 0.5 to 0.9 V and fail.

A pass figure that good work cannot meet either sends you re-crimping sound joints or teaches you to ignore the test - and this is the test that finds a bad crimp on a cable that can carry hundreds of amps.

The ground side matters for a second reason: the starter interlock reads the gear switch against the engine block, and its margin was budgeted on no more than 0.5 V between battery - and the block while cranking (D-408); the first real crank on the new harness measures that separately (check CK14). Nobody has measured this car's cranking current, and the cable lengths are still estimates until the measurement day.
options:
(a) Judge the joints, not the cable. While cranking, put the meter across each single joint in turn - one lead on the cable's copper or lug barrel, the other on the stud it bolts to - and each must read 0.1 V or less. The two end-to-end readings are still entered (E43, E44) and compared with the cable's own resistance, and fail by themselves only above 1.0 V. Costs nothing but a few more cranks, and a fail points at the joint to redo. The 0.1 V per joint is the usual workshop rule, not a figure from this car's documents.
(b) Keep 0.5 V end to end on both sides. Costs nothing and matches the interlock's budget on the ground side, but a sound cable of this length will probably fail it, so a fail tells you little.
(c) Scale the pass to the current. Buy a DC clamp meter that reads 600 A (about 40 to 60 USD, not in any cart), read the cranking current, and pass when the drop is no more than that current times the cable's own resistance plus 0.1 V. The most exact, and the meter also takes the sleeping-current reading later; it costs the meter and one more tool to learn.
recommend: (a), unless you want the cranking current known for its own sake - then (c)
stops: The pass lines of the first start on the new cables (E12, with its readings E43 and E44) and the re-check after the first drives (E33). The cables can still be built and the readings taken; only what counts as a fail waits.

title: Parts and tools the step-by-step list found missing
ask: May the parts and tools listed here go on the parts list - about 350 USD in all, by estimate - and may the bench items among them be bought now, before the freeze?
why:
Writing every step out showed things the steps use that no parts row buys, and four parts already on the list that the bench work before the freeze needs but that were not in the before-the-freeze purchase you approved (D-490). Every figure below is an estimate until a cart shows the price.

Missing from the list (new money, about 140 to 200 USD):
1. A fire extinguisher for the garage, 2.5 lb ABC or larger. The safety row names none. About 25 to 45.
2. A torque wrench in the foot-pound range (3/8 drive, about 10 to 80 ft-lb). The torque rule asks for one for the battery posts and the ground studs; the only wrench on the list stops at 20 N.m (15 ft-lb). About 40 to 60.
3. A long meter lead: about 25 ft of wire with a clip at each end, for the cranking voltage-drop readings between the battery in the back and the starter. Under 10, or made from the wire spools.
4. One more Deutsch 4-way plug kit and one more 6 AWG lug, so the practice crimps do not use up parts the car needs. About 10.
5. The size-12 contact removal tool. It is on the list at quantity 0; one is needed. About 12.
6. A 12 V bench supply of 5 A or more with leads, to run the power module on the desk before it is in the car - or no supply, and it runs off the car's battery on a fused lead. About 40 to 60, or nothing.

Already on the list, wanted earlier than planned (about 180 USD):
7. The USB-to-CAN cable (P138, about 90 for the module maker's own - confirm) and the terminal crimper for the power module's plug (P039, about 80). The bench rows that come before the interior strip - the sleep-current reading and the CAN export proof - need both.
8. The two memory chips for the display's Teensy (P108, about 10) and the clock's coin cell (P202, about 3). Without the chips the display firmware stops at boot, so the card and logging rows cannot be done.
options:
(a) Add all of it, and buy items 6, 7 and 8 now with the bench kit. About 350 USD in all, about 230 of it now. Nothing waits.
(b) Add all of it, but take item 6 as the free version: the module runs off the car's battery on a fused lead, no bench supply. About 300 in all, about 180 now. The module can then only be powered beside the car.
(c) Add items 1 to 5 only and buy nothing more before the freeze. About 100 to 140. The bench rows that need the module powered and its plug crimped, and the card and logging rows, move to after the freeze - and the interior strip waits on them today, so those rows would have to be re-ordered first.
recommend: (a), unless a bench supply is one more thing on the desk than you want - then (b)
stops: Buying for the bench session (the sleep-current reading R6 and the CAN export proof F-009), the card and logging rows (T-049, BT4), and the tool list of the backbone weekends (E8 to E12). Nothing else waits on it.
